paper_title: LLaDA MoE v2: Scaling Mixture-of-Experts Diffusion Language Models

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Diffusion language models (dLLMs) offer an alternative to autoregressive (AR) language modeling, yet the scaling behavior of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) dLLMs remains poorly understood. We systematically characterize how optimization hyperparameters, compute allocation, and architecture scale for MoE dLLMs, identifying quantitative differences from scaling trends previously reported for AR models. Specifically, for optimization, the optimal nominal batch size grows faster, while the optimal learning rate decays more rapidly with compute. For model--data allocation, IsoFLOP analysis reveals a slight data-side tilt: the optimal token budget grows faster than activated model-side computation. For MoE architecture, larger scales increasingly favor larger expert pools at fixed activated capacity, while moderate expert granularity remains consistently effective and the preferred fraction of activated capacity assigned to shared experts remains stable across scales. Guided by these findings, we train LLaDA MoE v2, a 30B-A3B dLLM, from scratch on 23.5T tokens. With approximately 65\% as many pretraining tokens as Qwen3, LLaDA MoE v2 approaches Qwen3 on several knowledge, reasoning, and coding benchmarks. After supervised fine-tuning alone, it outperforms SDAR Chat on seven of eight reasoning and coding benchmarks and remains close to Qwen3 on several tasks. These results establish practical scaling laws and design principles for MoE dLLMs.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Large language models (Zhao et al., 2026) have advanced largely through scale: as models, data, and compute grow, performance improves in systematic and predictable ways (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022). Most of this progress has followed the autoregressive (AR) paradigm (Radford et al., 2018; 2019; Brown et al., 2020; Ouyang et al., 2022), which factorizes the distribution of text sequence into next-token conditionals along fixed left-to-right order. Diffusion language models (dLLMs) (Lou et al., 2023; Sahoo et al., 2024; Ou et al., 2025; Nie et al., 2026b) offer an alternative probabilistic formulation: they define the distribution through an iterative denoising process, in which bidirectional model reconstructs the masked tokens of corrupted sequence, allowing multiple tokens to be decoded in parallel at each step (Wu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026). Recent dLLMs now match the capabilities of strong AR models, both when trained from scratch (Nie et al., 2025; 2026b;a) and when adapted from pretrained AR checkpoints (Bie et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025), making them promising candidate for future language modeling. Realizing this potential, however, requires understanding how dLLMs behave as training budgets grow. Existing scaling studies of dLLMs have so far focused on dense architectures (Nie et al., 2025; Ni et al., 2025b; von Rutte et al., 2026; Sahoo et al., 2026). MoE dLLMs have therefore begun to emerge (Zhu et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026), but their designs largely inherit AR practice. AR experience provides useful prior, but it cannot be assumed to transfer directly: dLLMs optimize masked denoising objective rather than next-token prediction, supervision falls only on masked positions, and each prediction conditions on corrupted sequence rather than causal prefix. Consequently, the scaling behavior of MoE dLLMs remains undercharacterized. In this work, we systematically characterize the scaling behavior and architectural design of MoE dLLMs across compute scales. We ask how the optimal batch size and learning rate change with compute, how fixed compute budget should be allocated between activated model-side computation and training tokens, and how the resulting activated budget should be decomposed into routing sparsity, expert granularity, and shared capacity. Table 1 summarizes the resulting empirical findings and the corresponding evidence. Across these dimensions, AR experience provides useful prior but requires dLLM-specific calibration. These findings yield practical guidance for scaling MoE dLLMs, which we validate by training LLaDA MoE v2, 30B-A3B model, from scratch on 23.5T tokens. LLaDA MoE v2 approaches Qwen3 30B-A3B (Yang et al., 2025) on several knowledge, reasoning, and coding benchmarks while using approximately 65% as many pretraining tokens, and matches prior MoE dLLM (Zhu et al., 2025) developed without such guidance at fraction of its training compute. Standard SFT turns it into strong instruct model: LLaDA MoE v2 outperforms SDAR Chat 30B-A3B (Cheng et al., 2026a) on seven of eight reasoning and coding benchmarks and remains competitive with Qwen3 across multiple benchmarks despite Qwen3s additional RL stage.

sections.title: 2.2 MIXTURE-OF-EXPERTS TRANSFORMERS AND SCALING LAWS
sections.content: A Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Transformer decouples model capacity from per-token computation by replacing the feed-forward network with ne routed experts and lightweight router (Jacobs et al., 1991; Shazeer et al., 2017; Lepikhin et al., 2020; Fedus et al., 2022; Zoph et al., 2022; Dai et al., 2024): the total parameter count scales with ne, whereas each token is processed by only small subset of them. Concretely, the router activates the top-na routed experts for each token and combines their outputs. In addition, every token is processed by single shared expert with intermediate width dshare = nsdexpert, where ns denotes shared capacity measured in units of one routed expert. We parameterize such an architecture by three variables: the activation ratio = (na + ns)/(ne + ns), which is the fraction of expert capacity activated per token; the expert granularity = 2dmodel/dexpert, which controls how routed capacity is partitioned into experts; and the shared-expert ratio = ns/(na + ns), which controls the fraction of activated expert capacity assigned to the shared pathway (Krajewski et al., 2024; Abnar et al., 2025; Tian et al., 2026). Scaling laws use small-scale measurements to estimate how compute-dependent choices, including optimization hyperparameters, modeldata allocation, and architecture, should change at larger budgets (Hestness et al., 2017; Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022; Krajewski et al., 2024; Abnar et al., 2025). In practice, power-law fits model the optimal batch size and learning rate as functions of the compute budget C, while IsoFLOP analysis fixes and sweeps model-side computation against training tokens (Hoffmann et al., 2022; Bi et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025a). Dense-model studies commonly approximate training compute as 6N D, where is the number of non-embedding parameters and is the number of training tokens, assuming that all parameters participate in processing each token (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022). Because this assumption does not hold for MoE models, we follow prior MoE scaling studies and use = D, where denotes activated non-embedding training FLOPs per token (Bi et al., 2024; Ludziejewski et al., 2025; Tian et al., 2026); full compute expressions are provided in Appendix A.1.

sections.title: 3 SCALING LAWS FOR MOE DLLMS
sections.content: In this section, we develop scaling framework for MoE dLLMs in three stages. We first calibrate compute-dependent batch size and learning rate, then estimate the optimal allocation between activated model-side computation and training data, and finally decompose the resulting model-side budget into activation ratio, expert granularity, and shared-expert ratio.

sections.title: 3.1 SCALING LAW FOR HYPERPARAMETERS
sections.content: Although hyperparameter scaling has been extensively studied for AR models (Bi et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025a), whether the same compute-dependent laws describe dLLMs remains an open question. Unlike AR training, which optimizes next-token prediction over causal prefixes, dLLMs are trained with masked denoising objective over partially observed sequences. Since each update supervises only sampled masked positions, the nominal token batch size does not directly correspond to the effective number of prediction targets; for example, under common uniform timestep sampling, only half of the tokens are predicted in expectation. This reduced effective supervision can change the gradient noise level, optimization stability, and learning-rate sensitivity. We therefore study how the optimal batch size and learning rate vary with compute, both to compare their scaling behavior with AR expectations and to establish stable, compute-efficient settings for the subsequent analyses. Concretely, we perform hyperparameter search over nominal token batch size and learning rate across set of representative model scales, ranging from 158M to 3.6B, under compute budgets from 1018 to 3 1020; the detailed training and model settings are provided in Appendix A.3. 3 Preprint. sections.title: 3.3 SCALING LAW FOR MOE ARCHITECTURE
sections.content: Translating this fixed budget into an MoE architecture poses dLLM-specific design problem because the router acts on masked denoising states that vary with noise level and mask pattern. We consider the three architectural dimensions defined in Section 2: the activation ratio A, which controls routing sparsity and thereby the size of the routed expert pool; the expert granularity G, which trades off routing diversity against per-expert capacity; and the shared-expert ratio S, which determines the fraction of activated capacity assigned to shared pathway. We examine how these dimensions should be configured across compute scales. For each reference compute scale C, we fix the activated model-side budget to (C) and sweep one architectural dimension at time while holding the other two fixed. Detailed settings are provided in Appendix A.5. Figure 4 summarizes these controlled architecture sweeps. Activation ratio: larger scales favor sparser activation. We examine the activation ratio in Figure 4(a). Under the fixed activated model-side budget (C), reducing generally lowers training loss, with the benefit becoming more pronounced as compute increases. At the smallest budgets, however, the second-lowest activation ratio slightly outperforms the sparsest setting. This exception is consistent with the intuition that extremely sparse routing exposes larger routed expert 6 Preprint. pool, which may require sufficient training compute to be effectively optimized. The trend suggests that MoE dLLMs can increasingly exploit this expert capacity at larger scales. Expert granularity: = 816 is robust. We next examine expert granularity in Figure 4(b). does not show monotonic trend across compute scales, suggesting that it is not primary scaling direction. Instead, it mainly reflects trade-off between routing diversity and per-expert capacity: coarser experts provide stronger individual transformations but fewer routing choices, while finergrained experts increase routing choices at the cost of narrower experts. For MoE dLLMs, this trade-off is relevant because masked denoising requires both diverse specialization over corrupted contexts and sufficient expert expressiveness. Empirically, = 8 to = 16 provides robust range in our sweep, although the exact optimum does not vary systematically with compute. Shared-expert ratio: = 33.3% remains optimal. We examine the shared-expert ratio in Figure 4(c). Across all compute scales, the loss curves are U-shaped and reach their minima at = 33.3%. This optimum contrasts with AR MoE designs: DeepSeekMoE adopts = 25%, Qwen3 uses no shared experts (Dai et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025), and Tian et al. (2026) report decreasing optimal ratio from 16.7% to 8.3%, motivating fixed one shared expert rule. Our dLLM sweeps instead favor shared pathway whose capacity grows proportionally with the activated model budget, rather than fixed shared component whose relative contribution diminishes with scale. We therefore derive dLLM-specific rule distinct from the AR heuristic: maintain approximately one unit of shared activated capacity for every two units of routed activated capacity. Our architecture sweeps translate the aggregate budget (C) into dLLM-specific architectural choices for routing over corrupted states that vary with noise level and mask pattern rather than causal prefixes. At fixed (C), larger scales favor sparser activation, while moderate expert granularity and stable shared-capacity fraction remain robust across the studied scales.

sections.title: 4 TRAINING LARGE-SCALE MOE DLLMS
sections.content: Guided by the scaling laws derived above, we design LLaDA MoE v2, 30B-A3B MoE dLLM, and train it on 23.5T tokens. We briefly introduce its architecture and training strategies below, with additional details provided in Appendix B. Model. LLaDA MoE v2 has 30B total parameters, with 3B parameters activated per token. Based on our scaling analysis, we adopt (A, G, S) = (9.09%, 8, 33.3%). Each layer comprises 128 finegrained routed experts with top-8 routing and one shared expert of width 4dexpert, corresponding to ns = 4 and yielding = (8 + 4)/(128 + 4) = 9.09% and = 4/(8 + 4) = 33.3%. Training strategy. We train LLaDA MoE v2 in five stages. Stages 1 and 2 each use 10T tokens, followed by 2T tokens of annealing in Stage 3. In Stage 4, we increase the RoPE base from 10,000 to 500,000, extend the context length from 4K to 32K, and continue training for 500B tokens. Stage 5 concludes with 1T tokens of long-context annealing, yielding the final pretrained base model.

sections.title: 4.1 BENCHMARK RESULTS
sections.content: As shown in Table 3, we compare LLaDA MoE v2 30B-A3B with five representative dLLM and AR baselines. The closest scale-matched baselines are SDAR Sci and Qwen3 30B-A3B: the former is obtained by continued pretraining from Qwen3 (Cheng et al., 2026a), whereas the latter is strong AR MoE model (Yang et al., 2025). LLaDA MoE v2 is trained from scratch on 23.5T tokens, 63% of SDAR Scis 37.05T and 65% of Qwen3s 36T. Across all 15 benchmarks, LLaDA MoE v2 achieves the highest average among the evaluated dLLMs (58.60), outperforming SDAR Sci by 3.78 points and the smaller dLLM baselines by at least 12.44 points. Its advantage over SDAR Sci is particularly pronounced on coding benchmarks such as HumanEval (+16.46) and BigCodeBench (+7.98), despite being pretrained from scratch rather than initialized from an AR checkpoint. Compared with Qwen3, LLaDA MoE v2 shows larger gaps on the Chinese knowledge benchmarks CEval and CMMLU and on some coding tasks, but remains close on several reasoning and coding benchmarks, including OlympiadBench (2.22) and HumanEval (2.44). sections.title: 4.2 SUPERVISED FINE-TUNING
sections.content: The preceding experiments evaluate the capabilities of the pretrained LLaDA MoE v2 base model. We further examine whether this scaling-guided pretrained model can be effectively adapted to instruction following and complex reasoning through standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Starting from the LLaDA MoE v2 30B-A3B base checkpoint, we construct an instruct model and evaluate it on mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks. We fine-tune LLaDA MoE v2 for three epochs on 7M instructionresponse examples. For each example, we keep the prompt uncorrupted, apply the masking process in Equation 1 only to the response, and compute the denoising loss over the masked positions. We use batch size of 512 sequences and peak learning rate of 5.0 106, with linear warmup over the first 8% of steps. We do not apply reinforcement learning (RL) after SFT and leave its integration to future work. We compare the resulting model with Qwen3 30B-A3B no think and SDAR Chat 30B-A3B. As shown in Table 4, LLaDA MoE v2 outperforms SDAR Chat on all four reasoning benchmarks and three of the four code benchmarks. Despite using fewer pretraining tokens, without the additional RL used by Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025), LLaDA MoE v2 remains close to Qwen3 on AIME 24/25 (AIME, 2025), MBPP, and LiveCodeBench, and surpasses it on MultiPL-E. These results show that LLaDA MoE v2 acquires strong reasoning and coding capabilities through SFT alone.

sections.title: 5 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Diffusion Language Models (dLLMs) have recently emerged as new paradigm for language modeling (Austin et al., 2021a; Campbell et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2022; Gulrajani & Hashimoto, 2023; He et al., 2023; Lou et al., 2023; Shi et al., 2024; Xue et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025b; Nie et al., 2026b; Song et al., 2025; Labs et al., 2025). In particular, masked discrete diffusion models are viewed as potential alternatives to autoregressive (AR) models, as they can generate multiple tokens in parallel at each denoising step (Arriola et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026; Cheng et al., 2026b). Recent work has scaled dLLMs both by pretraining from scratch (Nie et al., 2026b; Zhu et al., 2025; 2026) and by adapting pretrained AR models (Gong et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025; Bie et al., 2025). Meanwhile, several studies have begun to characterize the scaling behavior of dLLMs (Nie et al., 2025; Ni et al., 2025b; von Rutte et al., 2026; Ni et al., 2025a; Sahoo et al., 2026), though most of them are confined to dense architectures. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) and Scaling Laws. By replacing single feed-forward network with multiple fine-grained experts and selectively activating only subset of parameters for each token, MoE architectures enable models to increase capacity without proportional increase in computation (Shazeer et al., 2017; Lepikhin et al., 2020; Fedus et al., 2022; Du et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2024; Dai et al., 2024). Building on scaling law research for language models (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022), recent studies have used scaling insights to guide the design of compute-efficient MoE architectures (Clark et al., 2022; Abnar et al., 2025; Ludziejewski et al., 2025), and several works have also applied MoE to dLLMs (Zhu et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2026). Existing MoE dLLMs, however, largely adopt architectural choices developed for AR models, leaving their optimization, compute allocation, and expert architecture scaling behavior largely uncharacterized. 9 Preprint.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: In this work, we characterize how optimization hyperparameters, modeldata allocation, and expert architecture scale for MoE dLLMs, finding that AR trends provide useful priors but require dLLM-specific calibration. These results yield practical design principles that guide the fromscratch training of LLaDA MoE v2 30B-A3B. The model approaches Qwen3 on several benchmarks with fewer pretraining tokens, while SFT alone, without RL, produces an instruct model that outperforms SDAR Chat on seven of eight reasoning and coding tasks. Our experiments vary the scaling dimensions separately and therefore do not capture their interactions. Nevertheless, the large-scale results demonstrate the practical value of scaling-law-guided MoE dLLM design.

sections.title: A SCALING LAWS FOR MOE DLLMS
sections.content: A.1 COMPUTE ACCOUNTING We distinguish total parameter count, activated parameter count, and the activated computation used in our scaling analysis. Let nlayer be the number of Transformer layers, dmodel the hidden size, the sequence length, and rkv = nkvheads/nheads the ratio of key-value heads to query heads. Each MoE layer contains ne routed experts, each with intermediate width dexpert, of which na are selected per token. In the implemented architecture, every token is additionally processed by single shared expert with intermediate width dshare. To express routed and shared capacity in common units, we define ns dshare/dexpert, or equivalently dshare = nsdexpert. Thus, ns denotes the shared capacity measured in units of one routed expert, rather than the physical number of shared experts. With SwiGLU (Shazeer, 2020), the three projection matrices contain 3dmodeldexpert parameters for each routed expert and 3dmodeldshare = 3nsdmodeldexpert parameters for the single shared expert. Ignoring biases and normalization parameters, the total and activated non-embedding parameter counts are Pnonemb = nlayer Pact,nonemb = nlayer (cid:2)2d2 (cid:2)2d2 model(1 + rkv) + dmodelne + 3dmodel(nedexpert + dshare)(cid:3) , model(1 + rkv) + dmodelne + 3dmodel(nadexpert + dshare)(cid:3) . (4) (5) The first term accounts for the query, key, value, and output projections; the second accounts for the router, which scores all ne routed experts for every token; and the final term accounts for the routed experts and the single shared expert. Substituting dshare = nsdexpert recovers the equivalent-unit forms 3dmodeldexpert(ne + ns) and 3dmodeldexpert(na + ns), respectively. We use an input embedding matrix and separate LM head matrix, each containing dmodel parameters for vocabulary size . Their combined 2V dmodel parameters are included when reporting total or activated parameter counts but excluded from the non-embedding quantities used below. We count one multiplyaccumulate as two FLOPs. The forward FLOPs per token of one layer are approximated by Fattn = 4d2 model(1 + rkv) + 4sdmodel, FMoE = 2dmodelne + 6dmodel(nadexpert + dshare), (6) (7) where the two terms in Fattn correspond to the attention projections and the two sequence-level attention matrix multiplications, respectively. The terms in FMoE account for routing, the selected routed experts, and the single shared expert. Approximating the backward pass as twice the forward pass, we define the activated non-embedding FLOPs per token as = 3nlayer (cid:2)4d2 model(1 + rkv) + 4sdmodel + 2dmodelne + 6dmodel(nadexpert + dshare)(cid:3) . The learning rate is linearly warmed up for 2,000 optimizer steps to the peak value η, allowing optimization to enter stable regime before the peak rate is held constant until the final 10% of the training compute and then decayed to 0.1η using cosine schedule. For each model scale, we jointly search the global nominal token batch size and peak learning rate η, while holding the architecture and training-token budget fixed within each compute setting. For each run, we define its loss as the average training loss over the final 0.5% of its allocated training FLOPs. At each compute budget, we identify the minimum average loss and regard configurations whose losses are no more than 0.25% above this minimum as near-optimal (Bi et al., 2024). We include all near-optimal configurations in loglog linear regressions of batch size and learning rate against C, yielding the final scaling laws. TRAINING LARGE-SCALE MOE DLLMS B.1 MODEL ARCHITECTURE We train LLaDA MoE v2 30B-A3B, large MoE dLLM whose detailed architecture is reported in Table 6. The routing rule, the combination of routed and shared expert outputs, and the auxiliary objectives follow Appendix A.2. The Transformer backbone contains 32 layers with hidden size 3072 and uses grouped-query attention (GQA) with 32 query heads and 4 key-value heads. The model uses vocabulary of 157,184 tokens. All Transformer layers use an MoE feed-forward block. To realize the architecture-scaling recommendations, we use ne = 128 routed experts, activate na = 8 of them per token, and allocate ns = 4 expert-width units to the single shared expert. Setting = 8 gives dexpert = dmodel/4 and hence dshare = 4dexpert = dmodel. This discrete configuration yields = (8 + 4)/(128 + 4) = 9.09% and = 4/(8 + 4) = 33.3%. B.2 PRETRAINING We pretrain LLaDA MoE v2 30B-A3B from scratch for total of 23.5T nominal tokens. The pretraining corpus is constructed from broad collection of high quality text gathered from the web. We apply standard data processing pipeline that collects the raw text, removes boilerplate and malformed or low quality documents, deduplicates repeated content, and filters harmful material. Throughout pretraining, we optimize the denoising objective in Equation 1; the routing procedure and auxiliary objectives follow Appendix A.2. The five-stage data schedule is summarized in Table 7. Stages 1 and 2 draw separate 10T-token samples from the same source corpus, with the Stage 2 mixture assigning slightly more weight to mathematical reasoning and code data. For Stage 3, we construct curated 1T-token annealing corpus after cleaning, deduplication, and harmful-content filtering, and train on it for two epochs, yielding 2T training tokens. Stages 4 and 5 primarily use long-form data with sequence lengths of up to 32K tokens. We train in BF16 precision using AdamW with (β1, β2) = (0.9, 0.95) and weight decay of 0.1 (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017). The global nominal token batch size is 33,554,432 tokens. Each stage uses separate learning-rate schedule that linearly warms up from zero to its stage-specific peak over the first 2,000 optimizer steps. During the final 10% of the allocated training compute in Stages 14, the learning rate is decayed to the peak rate of the following stage using cosine schedule; in Stage 5, it is decayed to 5.0 106 using the same schedule. The peak learning rates for Stages 15 are 1.5 104, 1.0 104, 5.0 105, 1.0 105, and 7.0 106, respectively. B.3 SUPERVISED FINE-TUNING Starting from the final pretrained checkpoint, we fine-tune LLaDA MoE v2 30B-A3B for three epochs on 7M instructionresponse examples, primarily comprising single-turn mathematical reasoning and code generation tasks. We process the data following the same general procedure used for pretraining, removing malformed or low quality examples, deduplicating repeated content, and filtering harmful material, and then format every example using unified conversation template. The formatted examples are packed into non-overlapping 8K-token training sequences. For each instructionresponse pair, we concatenate the prompt and response but apply the forward masking process in Equation 1 only to response tokens, leaving the prompt available as uncorrupted conditioning context and computing the denoising loss only at masked response positions. The MoE load balancing loss and router z-loss described in Appendix A.2 remain active during SFT, with their coefficients unchanged at αaux = 0.01 and αz = 0.001. We update all model parameters using AdamW with (β1, β2) = (0.9, 0.999), weight decay of 0.1, and gradient clipping at maximum norm of 1.0. The global batch size is 512 sequences. The learning rate is linearly warmed up to 5.0 106 over the first 8% of training steps and then follows cosine schedule that decays it to minimum of 1.0 106. We use the final checkpoint as the instruct model and apply no reinforcement learning stage after SFT. B.4 EVALUATION We evaluate LLaDA MoE v2 across diverse suite of benchmarks covering general tasks (MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2020), MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024), CEval (Huang et al., 2023), CMMLU (Li et al., 2024), HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019), KorBench (Ma et al., 2025)), mathematical reasoning (GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021), OlympiadBench (He et al., 2024)), and code generation (CRUXEval (Gu et al., 2024), MBPP (Austin et al., 2021b), MultiPL-E (Cassano et al., 2022), HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), LiveCodeBench (Jain et al., 2025), BigCodeBench (Zhuo et al., 2025)). For the base-model results in Table 3, we use conditional likelihood for multiple-choice tasks and conditional generation for the remaining tasks, whereas all results in the SFT evaluation in Table 4 are obtained through conditional generation. For each model, we preferentially report results from its official publication (Yang et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2026a; Zhu et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025; Nie et al., 2026b); when benchmark result is unavailable, we report the score obtained under our unified evaluation configuration. We use conditional likelihood on MMLU, MMLU-Pro, CEval, CMMLU, and HellaSwag. For each example, we compute the conditional likelihood of every candidate answer given the prompt, select the candidate with the highest likelihood, and report accuracy over the benchmark. For an AR model, we compute the conditional log-likelihood under its left-to-right factorization. For LLaDA MoE v2, we follow the likelihood-evaluation protocols used in SMDM, LLaDA, and the previous LLaDA MoE (Nie et al., 2025; 2026b; Zhu et al., 2025). For SDAR, we estimate conditional likelihood using the method introduced in Block Diffusion (Arriola et al., 2025). 20 Preprint. For conditional-generation tasks, each model generates completion from the benchmark prompt using its native generation procedure. For code tasks, we extract the code from the response and execute it against the benchmark test cases. For mathematical reasoning tasks, we extract the final answer and determine correctness using the equivalence checker. All instruct models are evaluated through conditional generation. We allow at most 1,024 generated tokens on each benchmark. Because this limit can be insufficient for models to produce final answer on MATH, OlympiadBench, AIME 2024, and AIME 2025, we increase the limit to 4,096 tokens for these benchmarks. LLaDA MoE v2 uses semi-autoregressive sampling (Nie et al., 2026b) with block size of 64 and total number of denoising steps equal to the generation length. For SDAR, we follow its recommended block diffusion decoding procedure with block size of 4 and likewise set the total number of sampling steps to the generation length (Cheng et al., 2026a).
